lead: A satellite does not hand you a map. It hands you a grid of digital numbers. Digital image processing turns that raw grid into a corrected image, stretches and filters it so the eye can read it, and then asks a computer to sort every pixel into a class — water, crop, built-up. A final error matrix says how much to trust the labels. District crop surveys, urban growth studies and flood damage maps all depend on this chain.
prereq: You need the spectral signatures of 6.3, the resolutions of 6.5, and the visual keys of 6.6, which become the training classes.

blocks.text: A digital image is a grid of square pixels. Each pixel holds a digital number (DN) — a whole number stored at the radiometric resolution of the sensor, 0 to 255 for an 8-bit image. One grid is one band. A multispectral image stacks several bands pixel for pixel, so band 3 and band 4 at row 120, column 45 describe the same patch of ground.

Radiometric correction fixes brightness. Sensor calibration removes detector drift using known on-board references. Sun angle correction divides reflectance by the cosine of the solar zenith angle, because a low winter sun or a slope tilted away receives less energy and would look falsely dark. Haze correction subtracts path radiance, the light scattered into the sensor by the atmosphere, which lifts even the darkest pixel above zero.

Geometric correction fixes position. Ground control points (GCPs) are features — a road junction, a tank bund, a bridge — whose image coordinates and map coordinates are both known. A transformation is fitted through them and the image is resampled onto the map grid. Nearest neighbour copies the closest original DN and keeps values intact. Bilinear interpolation takes the four nearest input pixels and averages them with weights that fall with distance, so the result looks smoother but invents new DN values.

A histogram counts how many pixels carry each DN. A raw scene often fills only a narrow slice of the range because of haze or weak contrast, so it looks grey and flat. A linear contrast stretch pulls the used range out to the full display range.

blocks.where: DN(in) is the input digital number; min and max are the lowest and highest values kept, read from the histogram; DN(out) is the stretched value, clipped to 0–255; 255 is the top of an 8-bit display.

blocks.text: Histogram equalisation is a stronger, non-linear stretch. It reassigns values so every brightness level holds roughly the same number of pixels. Detail in dark forest opens up, but noise in a clear reservoir can be exaggerated.

A spatial filter slides a small kernel, usually 3 × 3, across the image. A low-pass kernel gives every cell the weight 1/9; the output is the average of the nine cells in the window, the centre pixel included, which smooths noise and blurs edges. A high-pass kernel puts a large positive weight at the centre and negative weights around it; flat ground cancels to near zero and only edges survive, so the image looks sharpened.

A false colour composite loads three bands into the red, green and blue channels of the display. The usual choice sends near-infrared to red, red to green and green to blue. Healthy vegetation reflects strongly in the near-infrared, so it appears bright red, while water stays dark.

A band ratio divides one band by another, pixel by pixel. Dividing cancels much of the illumination difference between a sunlit slope and a shaded one, so the ratio shows the material rather than the light falling on it.

blocks.where: ρ(NIR) and ρ(red) are reflectance or DN in the near-infrared and red bands; NDVI runs from −1 to +1; healthy crops approach 0.8, bare soil about 0.2, water and shadow are negative, and thick cloud stays close to zero.

blocks.text: Principal component analysis (PCA) rotates the bands into new uncorrelated axes called components, ordered by variance. The first component carries most of the brightness, later ones carry subtle spectral differences. Only a few universities teach the eigenvector working in full; know what the method is for.
Vegetation indices drive crop monitoring, drought watch and forest cover work. Ratios of red and near-infrared also separate iron-rich rock from vegetation in geological mapping.

In supervised classification the analyst draws training areas for each class, using the visual keys from 6.6. Software computes the mean and covariance of every class. The maximum likelihood rule then assigns each pixel to the class with the highest probability, assuming the class values follow a normal distribution.

In unsupervised classification there are no training areas. The k-means algorithm picks k clusters, seeds a mean for each, assigns every pixel to the nearest mean, recomputes the means, and repeats until the means stop moving. The analyst then names the clusters — water, crop, built-up — by looking at them on the image.

Supervised gives named classes directly and needs ground knowledge; unsupervised finds groups the analyst may not have expected and needs labelling afterwards. After classification, a majority filter removes isolated single pixels, and the classes are labelled on the map.

Accuracy is judged against test pixels checked on the ground, listed in an error matrix of classes mapped against classes true. Overall accuracy is the diagonal sum divided by the total. Kappa removes the agreement that chance alone would produce.

blocks.where: p(o) is the observed agreement, the fraction of test pixels on the diagonal; p(e) is the agreement expected by chance from the row and column totals; κ = 1 is perfect agreement, κ = 0 is chance level.

examples.question: One band has digital numbers from 40 to 90. It is stretched linearly to the full 0–255 range. Write the stretch formula, find the output for input DN 40, 65 and 90, and state what happens to a pixel with DN 30.
steps: Read the ends from the histogram: min = 40 and max = 90, so the range is 90 − 40 = 50.
Write the stretch: DN(out) = (DN(in) − 40) ÷ 50 × 255, which is 5.1 × (DN(in) − 40).
Input 30: (30 − 40) ÷ 50 × 255 = −10 ÷ 50 × 255 = −51, which is outside the display range and is clipped to 0.
examples.answer: The stretch gives DN 40 → 0, DN 65 → 127.5 (stored as 128) and DN 90 → 255; any DN below 40 clips to 0.

traps: High overall accuracy does not remove class confusion. Read the error matrix by row and column. A class can be 95 per cent correct on the diagonal (user's accuracy) and yet have a low producer's accuracy, because many of its own ground pixels were labelled as another class. Check both directions before trusting any single class.
Radiometric correction is about brightness, geometric correction about position. Marks are lost by swapping the two.
A contrast stretch changes only the display values, not the stored reflectance. Do not claim it corrects the image.
NDVI is (NIR − red) ÷ (NIR + red). Reversing the order gives a negative index and a wrong map, and water genuinely has a negative NDVI.

quiz.q: Define digital number and give the DN range of an 8-bit image.
quiz.a: The value stored in one pixel of one band; 0 to 255 for 8-bit.

quiz.q: Why does a raw image often look flat, and why does haze lift the darkest DN above zero?
quiz.a: The scene fills only a narrow part of the DN range, so contrast is low. Atmospheric scattering adds a near-constant path radiance to every pixel, so the minimum stays above zero.

quiz.q: A 3 × 3 low-pass kernel with all weights 1/9 covers a window of eight pixels with DN 10 and a centre pixel with DN 50. Find the output.
Near-infrared reflectance is 0.50 and red reflectance is 0.10. Find NDVI.
State two differences between supervised and unsupervised classification.
quiz.a: Supervised needs training areas chosen by the analyst and yields named classes directly. Unsupervised groups pixels by spectral similarity and needs the analyst to name the clusters afterwards.

quiz.q: A map reports 90 per cent overall accuracy but kappa 0.35. What does this tell you?
quiz.a: Much of the agreement could be chance, usually because one dominant class fills most of the map. Check the error matrix rows and columns for confused classes before trusting the map.

quiz.q: A district map must separate three similar crops. Which enhancement and which classifier would you try, and how would you judge the result?
quiz.a: Use NDVI and a false colour composite to test separability, plus a contrast stretch for display. Try maximum likelihood with well-spread training areas, and judge by class-wise accuracies and kappa, not overall accuracy alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Operational crop forecasting, forest inventories and urban planning now run on regular classification pipelines, and machine-learning classifiers such as random forests and support vector machines have largely replaced maximum likelihood in research. Cloud platforms let one analyst classify a whole state from a laptop. Accuracy assessment has become the formal part of the job, because a map without a stated error cannot be used by a planner.
